# Tobit Chapter 2 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, Tobit 2 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/TOB_002_page_001.jpg

---

**1** Under the new king Esarhaddon, I was able to come home. Anna was there waiting for me, and so was Tobias. We had a good life again for a while. When the feast of Weeks came around — Pentecost — I had a fine meal prepared and sat down with my family.

**2** The table was set. There was plenty to eat. But before I touched a bite, I turned to Tobias: "Son, go out and find one of our people — someone poor, someone who still holds God in his heart — and bring him back. I'll wait for you. We'll eat together."

**3** Tobias went looking. He came back with nothing — but he had news. "Father, one of our own people has been murdered and thrown into the marketplace. He's still lying there."

**4** I didn't touch my food. I jumped up right away, carried the body inside, and laid him in a side room to wait until sundown.

**5** Then I came back, washed up, and sat down to eat my meal. But I could not taste a thing. Grief had taken my appetite.

**6** The words of Amos came back to me: "Your feasts shall be turned to mourning, all your songs to lamentation." I wept.

**7** At sunset I went out, dug a grave, and buried him properly.

**8** My neighbors shook their heads and laughed. "He still hasn't learned his lesson. He had to run for his life once already because of this, and now he's back at it — burying bodies again."

**9** That night, after washing up, I went out to sleep in the courtyard. It was hot, and I lay down near the wall with my face turned up to the sky.

**10** I had no idea there were sparrows nesting in the wall just above me. Their droppings fell into my open eyes while I slept. By morning, white films had formed across both eyes. I was blind. I went from doctor to doctor — none of them could do anything for me. Through all of this, my nephew Achiacharus kept us fed, until he had to leave for Elymais.

**11** With Achiacharus gone, Anna had to find work. She took on weaving and needlework — skilled labor, contracted to local employers. She worked hard for every coin. In the month of Dystros, when she finished a weaving job and delivered it,

**12** her employers paid her full wages — and, as a bonus, gave her a young goat to take home.

**13** When she walked through the door, the goat started bleating. I heard it and called out: "Anna, where did that animal come from? It's stolen, isn't it? You need to give it back. We don't keep stolen goods — we don't eat stolen goods. That's not who we are."

**14** "It's a gift," she said. "They gave it to me on top of my wages. A gift, Tobit." I didn't believe her. I kept pushing, kept insisting she send it back. The argument turned ugly. Then Anna looked at me and said — and every word hit home: "Where's all that mercy of yours now? Where are your famous righteous deeds? The whole world knows what you've become!"

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

- Verse 1: PNEUMA opens with a brief establishing context ("We had a good life again") to help readers track the narrative timeline. The feast sets up the bitter interruption to follow.
- Verse 3: "murdered" — PNEUMA uses this rather than "strangled" to make the violence immediate for modern readers. The Greek pepnigmenos (strangled) is more specific but can read clinically.
- Verse 10: "I was blind" — PNEUMA adds this summary sentence for narrative clarity. The blindness is the hinge of the entire plot; readers need to feel its full weight.
- Verse 14: The final exchange between Tobit and Anna is one of the most emotionally charged moments in the book. Anna's words are devastating — she turns Tobit's piety back on him as an indictment. PNEUMA renders this with maximum rhetorical impact: "every word hit home."
- The irony of chapter 2 is structural: Tobit's very righteousness (burying the dead) leads to his blindness; his very righteousness (refusing stolen goods) leads to his domestic humiliation. PNEUMA tries to make both ironies felt.

*— PNEUMA*
